extracted.intended_audience: employers, unions, labor practitioners, HR professionals, and stakeholders affected by the NLRA joint-employer standard (including lawyers and business commentators)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and definition of 'employer' and 'joint employer' under the National Labor Relations Act, grounded in common-law agency principles and applied across representation and unfair-labor-practice contexts. The page explains the final rule's tests (including reserved and indirect control), an exhaustive list of essential terms and conditions of employment, and related limits (no industry exemptions, no presumptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law agency control standard for 'employer'
rubrics_metrics.description: All common-law cases ... focus on whether a common-law agency relationship exists, and control is the touchstone of that inquiry under the common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board is guided by Supreme Court decisions to consult the common law of agency when interpreting 'employer' in Section 2(2) of the Act; the inquiry centers on control rather than the tort/contract context of Restatement authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform application across representation and unfair-labor-practice contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of 'joint employer' applies in all contexts under the Act, including both the representation-case and unfair-labor-practice case context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No commenter suggested limiting the joint-employer standard to one context; the final rule's standard will be used in both representation and ULP proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all probative indicia including reserved and indirect control
rubrics_metrics.description: The common law requires the Board to evaluate 'all probative indicia of employer status' in determining whether entities are 'employers' or 'joint employers' under the Act, including forms of indirect and reserved control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with the D.C. Circuit in BFI v. NLRB, the Board will weigh both indirect and reserved control as relevant evidence in the joint-employer inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct supervision not a prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct supervision over an employee is not a necessary prerequisite to a finding of an employment relationship for purposes of the Act; Allied Chemical is inapposite to impose such a requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing in Allied Chemical or subsequent cases suggests a modification of ordinary common-law agency principles to require 'direct supervision' as a statutory prerequisite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'share or codetermine' (authority to control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (c) defined 'share or codetermine those matters governing employees' essential terms and conditions of employment' to mean 'for an employer to possess the authority to control (whether directly, indirectly, or both), or to exercise the power to control (whether directly, indirectly, or both), one or more of the employees' essential terms and conditions of employment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'matters' refers to workplace issues related to those terms; the standard focuses on possession or exercise of authority to control (directly or indirectly) over essential terms and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession (reserved) of authority to control is probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Reservation of authority to control essential terms or conditions of employment is an important consideration under common-law agency principles and can establish joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractual allocations of control (including 'boilerplate' reservations) have legal force without regard to whether authority was actually exercised; examples include Jewel Tea Co. and Value Village, which treated contractually reserved powers as sufficient to find joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control (control through an intermediary) can be probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of indirect control over essential terms or conditions of employment may be evidence of joint-employer status; an entity need not itself actually exercise control over particular employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Restatement (Second) of Agency, the subservant doctrine, and BFI v. NLRB support weighing indirect control; control exercised through intermediaries can be relevant in determining employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over one essential term or condition can suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: Control over one essential term or condition of employment (e.g., wages) can be sufficient to create an employment relationship or to establish joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board does not construe 'matters' to require control of multiple essential terms; given the centrality of wages, control over wages alone could be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession versus exercise: possession can be determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer's possession of the authority to control (even if unexercised) can be evidence of an employment relationship and joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard that turns solely on ex-post exercise of reserved authority would impede parties' ability to assess ex ante whether they will have obligations under the Act; reserved authority thus has legal significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive list of essential terms and conditions of employment (final rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule incorporates an exhaustive list of essential terms and condition[s] of employment: '(1) wages, benefits, and other compensation; (2) hours of work and scheduling; (3) the assignment of duties to be performed; (4) the supervision of the performance of duties; (5) work rules and directions governing the manner, means, and methods of the performance of duties and the grounds for discipline; (6) the tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge; and (7) working conditions related to the safety and health of employees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These listed items are threshold matters that, if an entity possesses authority to control or exercises power to control one or more, may give rise to a finding that the entity is a joint employer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of hours of work and scheduling as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Hours of work and scheduling are included among the essential terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Restatement and Board law treat scheduling as probative of joint-employer status; scheduling is often intertwined with hours of work. Commenters raised industry-specific concerns (manufacturing, staffing) about burdens from treating scheduling as essential, but the Board retained it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of workplace health and safety as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Working conditions related to the safety and health of employees are included as an essential term and condition of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although subject to extensive regulatory schemes, control over workplace health and safety is indicative of joint-employer status; contractual clauses that merely incorporate regulatory requirements without reserving authority are not indicative of joint-employer status. The Covid-19 pandemic underscores the importance of this inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of work rules and directions governing manner, means, or methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Work rules and directions governing the manner, means, or methods of work performance and the grounds for discipline are essential terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possessing or exercising control over work rules/directions illuminates the extent of control an employer exercises over details of the work. Commenters warned this could sweep broadly and disproportionately affect certain industries; the Board retained the item based on Restatement support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between joint-employer status and bargaining scope; duty to bargain over mandatory subjects controlled
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an entity is found to be a joint employer because it possesses the authority to control or exercises the power to control one or more essential terms or conditions, that entity has a statutory duty to bargain over all mandatory subjects of bargaining it possesses the authority to control or exercises the power to control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of a joint employer's duty to bargain is distinct from joint-employer status; scope disputes will be assessed case-by-case using longstanding precedent. Paragraph (h) of the final rule clarifies the nature of the bargaining obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No industry- or size-specific exemptions; uniform application of the standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will apply common-law agency principles uniformly to all entities within its jurisdiction and declines to create industry-specific exclusions (e.g., construction, hospitals, franchises, cooperatives) or an across-the-board small-business exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No historical or textual basis in the Act for exempting particular groups; Board jurisdiction is based on interstate commerce thresholds present in the Act rather than minimum-employee thresholds used in other statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declines to adopt rebuttable presumptions for joint-employer status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board declined commenters' invitation to clarify that possession or exercise of certain forms of control would give rise to rebuttable presumptions of joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of presumptions, the Board relies on the detailed analysis of whether particular forms of control are material under common-law agency principles and will assess evidence case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 2020 rule's 'substantial direct and immediate control' restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board found the 2020 rule's reintroduction of control-based restrictions—specifically the requirement of 'substantial direct and immediate control'—to be contrary to common-law agency principles and rescinded that rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule codifies that indirect and reserved forms of control are relevant, restoring a view aligned with common-law agency precedent and judicial guidance (e.g., BFI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract provisions that merely incorporate regulatory requirements are not indicative
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractual terms that do nothing more than incorporate regulatory requirements, without otherwise reserving authority to control or exercising power to control performance or terms and conditions of employment, are not indicative of joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will distinguish between contractual clauses that allocate authority to control and clauses that simply restate regulatory obligations; the former can be probative, the latter generally are not.
